ai.definition: Body-Heat & Motion Harvesting is a technology that converts the thermal and mechanical energy generated by human body warmth and movement into electrical power using materials like thermoelectric or piezo films.
ai.howItWorks: Thermoelectric or piezoelectric films, when attached to the skin, generate electricity from the temperature difference between the skin and ambient air (thermoelectric) or from mechanical strain caused by body movements (piezoelectric). This process converts a small amount of thermal or mechanical energy into electrical microwatts.
ai.problemSolved: It addresses the need for self-sustaining power sources for wearable devices and medical implants, reducing reliance on batteries that require frequent replacement or charging.
ai.manufacturing: Manufacturing involves creating thin, flexible films using thermoelectric or piezoelectric materials. These films are then integrated into clothing or directly applied to the skin of wearables or medical devices.
ai.buildProcess: The build process includes material selection, film fabrication, integration with wearable devices or implants, and testing for efficiency and durability.
ai.costDrivers: Cost drivers include the quality and availability of thermoelectric or piezoelectric materials, manufacturing processes, and the complexity of integrating these films into existing wearable or implant designs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: promising but early stage with significant potential for development and commercialization
ai.regulation: Currently in a pre-commercial phase, so regulatory frameworks are not yet fully established. However, as the technology matures, it will likely require compliance with medical device regulations.
ai.risks: Technical risks include optimizing efficiency and ensuring long-term reliability of the films. Safety concerns may arise from potential skin irritation or allergic reactions to the materials used.
ai.profitability: Uncertain at this stage due to early development and lack of widespread commercial applications, but has the potential for significant market disruption in self-powered devices and medical implants.
ai.futureDevelopment: Future developments could include improving efficiency, reducing material costs, and expanding the range of applications beyond wearables and medical implants into broader consumer electronics.

glossary.def: A property where a material converts heat directly into electricity through the Seebeck effect.
A property where mechanical stress is converted into an electric charge, and vice versa.

subsystems.name: Thermal harvester
subsystems.role: converts the temperature difference between skin and air into a small voltage.

subsystems.name: Motion harvester
subsystems.role: converts body movement into electricity via piezoelectric or electrostatic effects.

subsystems.name: Power management
subsystems.role: rectifies and boosts the tiny, irregular output to a usable voltage.

subsystems.name: Energy storage
subsystems.role: buffers harvested energy for when the device needs more power than is being generated.

subsystems.name: Wearable integration
subsystems.role: packages the harvesters and electronics into a comfortable, skin-safe form.

subsystems.name: Load device
subsystems.role: the wearable or implant that uses the harvested power.

buildSteps.title: Design the harvester layout
buildSteps.detail: Choose body location (wrist, chest) and decide the mix of thermoelectric and motion harvesters based on available temperature gradient and movement.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate thermoelectric modules
buildSteps.detail: Dope and cut semiconductor legs (bismuth telluride), solder them between ceramic plates, and wire them in series to boost voltage.

buildSteps.title: Fabricate motion harvesters
buildSteps.detail: Deposit piezoelectric thin films on flexible substrates, pattern electrodes, and assemble cantilevers with a proof mass tuned to body-motion frequencies.

buildSteps.title: Assemble power management circuit
buildSteps.detail: Connect harvesters to a rectifier and a DC-DC converter that extracts maximum power and charges a storage element.

buildSteps.title: Integrate energy storage
buildSteps.detail: Attach a supercapacitor or thin-film battery to buffer energy for peak loads.

buildSteps.title: Encapsulate for wearability
buildSteps.detail: Seal the device in flexible, waterproof, skin-safe polymers; ensure good thermal contact for the thermoelectric module.

buildSteps.title: Test and calibrate
buildSteps.detail: Measure power output on a thermal manikin or human volunteer under typical conditions, and tune electronics for efficiency.

buildSteps.title: Connect to the load
buildSteps.detail: Integrate with the target device (e.g., a health sensor or watch) and verify continuous operation.

prerequisites.tech: Thermoelectric materials with high efficiency at small temperature differences
prerequisites.why: bismuth telluride is commercial, but performance is limited; better materials are still lab-stage.
PVDF and similar polymers are available, but generate only microwatts from body motion.
sensors and microcontrollers now run on microwatts, making harvested power useful.
commercial chips can boost millivolt inputs to usable levels.
small storage exists, but cycle life and capacity for wearables need improvement.

pathway.milestone: niche self-powered devices like thermoelectric watches and wireless sensors
pathway.unlocks: basic battery-free operation for very low-power devices.

pathway.milestone: wearable health monitors powered continuously by body heat and motion
hybrid harvesters reaching milliwatt output, enabling communication and displays
pathway.unlocks: more capable wearables and smart clothing.

pathway.milestone: implantable medical devices powered by the body itself
